blocks.text: Ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) spectroscopy is one of the most popular analytical techniques because it is versatile and easy to use. UV-Vis light is passed through a sample and the transmittance of the light (T) is measured; the absorbance (A) is found from A = -log T. A UV-Vis spectrum shows the absorbance of a substance at different wavelengths, and the absorbance at any wavelength depends on the electronic structure of the molecule.

A compound can have sigma electrons (in sigma bonds), pi electrons (in unsaturated compounds only) and n electrons (non-bonding, lone pairs). Sigma bonding orbitals are lowest in energy, pi bonding orbitals higher, and non-bonding orbitals higher still. When radiation of the right frequency is absorbed, an electron moves from one of these orbitals to an empty anti-bonding orbital, sigma* or pi*. UV-Vis spectroscopy uses wavelengths of about 200-800 nm. The important transitions are pi to pi*, n to pi* and n to sigma*.

blocks.alt: Energy-level diagram with an upward energy arrow. Levels from top: sigma* (anti-bonding) and pi* (anti-bonding), bracketed 'These are normally empty'; n (non-bonding), 'These contain lone pairs'; pi (bonding) and sigma (bonding), 'These contain normal bonding pairs of electrons'. Six upward arrows: from sigma to pi* and to sigma*, from pi to pi* and to sigma*, and from n to pi* and to sigma*.
blocks.caption: Figure 29.4: Transition of electrons from lower energy to higher energy levels (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 29.4).

blocks.text: Buta-1,3-diene, CH2=CH-CH=CH2, absorbs most strongly at 217 nm; the wavelength of maximum absorption is called lambda max. This is in the UV region, so no visible light is absorbed and the compound is colourless. It has no non-bonding electrons, so the only transitions measured are pi to pi*.

blocks.alt: Graph of absorbance (0 to 1.0) against wavelength (200 to 300 nm). The curve starts near 0.33 at 200 nm, rises to a peak of about 0.86 and falls to almost zero by 250 nm, staying flat to 300 nm. A label at the peak reads lambda max = 217 nm, with the note 'Maximum absorption at this wavelength'.
blocks.caption: Figure 29.5: Absorption spectrum of buta-1,3-diene (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 29.5).

blocks.text: Lambda max depends strongly on the extent of conjugation, as butadiene (217 nm), hexatriene (257 nm) and octatetraene (290 nm) show. In a conjugated system electrons are shared over a long chain; the more conjugated a compound, the more energy levels it has and the smaller the gaps between them. Smaller gaps need less energy, so light of lower frequency and longer wavelength is absorbed. Each extra conjugated double bond usually raises lambda max by about 30 to 40 nm, and highly conjugated compounds absorb visible light and are often brightly coloured.

blocks.alt: Skeletal formulas of three conjugated chains with alternating double and single bonds: butadiene (two double bonds) labelled 217 nm, hexatriene (three double bonds) labelled 257 nm and octatetraene (four double bonds) labelled 290 nm.
blocks.caption: Butadiene, hexatriene and octatetraene with their lambda max values (original drawing after the structures printed in 29.4).

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: A green tomato and a ripe red tomato have different colours: a green tomato has much chlorophyll, while a red tomato contains lycopene. The two compounds have different lambda max values and so specific colours in the visible range.
